prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enables measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My opening ballot put Halperin, Nelson and Young (B007) first, because defect-mediated two-step melting with a hexatic phase is the kind of simple, universal mechanism I trust. But I was the only member to rank it, and I have to take that seriously rather than treat my own taste as the committee's measure of merit. Reading the other seven ballots, the optical lattice clock (B004) is the one candidate where the scientific case is both strong and unusually clean. It rests on a single sharp idea, that a lattice at the magic wavelength cancels the light shift so that Doppler and recoil effects are removed while thousands of atoms are interrogated at once. That idea was turned into the most precise measurements ever made, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and these are now used to test constancy of constants, to resolve gravitational redshift over millimetres, and to prepare a redefinition of the second. It is understood, not merely working: the systematic shifts (blackbody radiation, higher-order lattice shifts, collisions) are controlled by well-posed theory that matches experiment. Katori proposed and first realised the lattice clock, and Ye's group drove the accuracy records and the many-body Fermi-degenerate clock, so a two-person prize maps onto two identifiable contributions with little attribution noise. Four members placed it first and a fifth in the top three, and unlike my own first choice that support comes from members whose arguments I can evaluate on the merits.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B004 is largely a refinement of an established paradigm, precision spectroscopy with trapped atoms, which the committee already honoured in 2005 (Hall and Hansch, frequency comb) and 2012 (Wineland, Haroche); one can argue the conceptual surprise is smaller than in a new phase of matter or a new window on the universe. The case rests on measurement performance, which is real but could be seen as engineering-driven, and the pending redefinition of the second means its largest practical consequence has not yet happened. There is also a modest attribution gap: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and others made decisive contributions, and a two-name prize sets a hard boundary. Finally, by moving off B007 I give up what I think is the deeper conceptual idea, but its overlap with the 2016 topological-defects prize and the near-absence of support for it make a standalone B007 prize hard to defend this year.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest example of a new measurement technique that redefines what can be measured: the magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping many atoms in the interrogation, giving uncertainties at the 1e-18 level beyond the caesium standard.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this, and it moved me. Where I would qualify it is in the weight put on being a measurement advance. The reason I now support B004 is not just that it is more precise but that the precision rests on a mechanism one can write down and analyse, the cancellation of the differential light shift at the magic wavelength, plus a controlled treatment of the residual shifts. I would therefore want the citation to name the lattice-trapping idea, not only the accuracy record, and I disagree with the implication that a record number alone makes a prize; the same standard applied to atom interferometry (B036), which you rank fourth, would favour it less because its credit is spread among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and others.

responses.point: The magic-wavelength lattice is a clean atomic-structure idea that turned into the most precise measurements ever made, testing fundamental physics and relativistic redshift, with Katori and Ye a natural two-person configuration though Lemonde and others contributed.
responses.response: This is persuasive to me, and as someone outside atomic physics I find the physical-mechanism framing helpful. I would press one point: the attribution to Katori for the concept and Ye for the performance frontier is correct but should be verified against the history of the first Sr lattice clock demonstrations, where Lemonde's group and Takamoto and Katori published within a short time. I would not let that block the prize, because the proposal priority is Katori's and the sustained frontier is Ye's, but the committee should record that choice explicitly rather than assume it is obvious.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a tunable platform with flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity, and Bistritzer-MacDonald plus Jarillo-Herrero is a natural theory-plus-experiment prize.
responses.response: I put B010 fourth and I share the enthusiasm for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction of the magic angle, which is a quantitative continuum-model result I admire. But I am less comfortable than you are that the three supplied names make a fair prize. Cao, the first author of the 2018 papers, is absent, and the field's explanation of the superconducting and correlated phases is still debated, so this is less mature in the sense that matters to me, namely whether the mechanism is understood. I keep it as an alternative, not a preferred choice, and think it becomes stronger in a few years if the pairing mechanism is settled.

responses.point: Circuit QED opened a new regime of strong coupling of an artificial atom to a single microwave photon and underlies essentially all superconducting quantum processors; the competition lies in whether Girvin joins the experimental pair and the lead theorist.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance of B034, and I recognise it is close to your own work. My reservation is attribution, not merit: four credited names, a 2004 proposal that Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf made jointly, and experiments by Wallraff and Schoelkopf mean any three-person cut excludes someone with a clear claim, which is a harder problem than the two-person B004. Given the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits already recognised the superconducting-circuit platform, I would also ask whether circuit QED is distinct enough for the committee to credit it so soon; I would rank it behind B004 for this reason but keep it open for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views B004 as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 trapped-ion prizes, or as an incremental extension.
Whether to credit Lemonde or other early lattice-clock groups, and how firmly Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength concept is established relative to contemporaneous work.

Whether B007 deserves a place in a later year given its overlap with the 2016 topological-defects prize and the historical role of experiments confirming the hexatic phase, which I have not examined closely.
How settled the pairing mechanism in magic-angle graphene must be before B010 is mature enough.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. My frequent co-authors and institutional ties (Gothenburg, MPI Stuttgart and Dresden, Oxford, Cornell, Göttingen) do not include any credited candidate on the shortlist. I note only that Göran Johansson and Eva Olsson are in the closely linked Chalmers environment, which is not a recusal matter.
